## Theoretical Expectations

The population follows:

$$
X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)
$$

```{r}
population_mean <- 0
population_variance <- 1
population_sd <- 1
population_skewness <- 0
population_excess_kurtosis <- 0
```

The population mean is 0 and the population standard deviation is 1. Because this is a Standard Normal population, its skewness and excess kurtosis are both 0.

The theoretical standard error is:

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\overline{X})
= \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

## Prediction for Standard Normal

Because the population is already normally distributed, I predict that the sampling distribution of the sample mean will be approximately normal for every sample size \(n\), including \(n=1\). Increasing \(n\) should reduce the standard error, but it should not be necessary to create normality.

## Original Population Distribution

```{r}
curve(
  dnorm(
    x,
    mean = population_mean,
    sd = population_sd
  ),
  from = -4,
  to = 4,
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2,
  main = "Standard Normal Population Distribution",
  xlab = "Population value",
  ylab = "Density"
)
```

The original population has the familiar symmetric, bell-shaped form of a normal distribution. It is centered at 0, and most values fall relatively close to 0.

## Reproducible Simulation Setup

The last four digits of my student ID are 4160, so I use 4160 as the seed. This makes my simulation reproducible.

```{r}
student_id <- 4160
reps <- 10000

broad_n_values <- c(
  1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100
)

population_generator <- function(n) {
  rnorm(
    n,
    mean = population_mean,
    sd = population_sd
  )
}

simulate_means <- function(n, reps = 10000) {
  replicate(
    reps,
    mean(population_generator(n))
  )
}

run_simulations <- function(n_values, reps = 10000) {
  
  results <- list()
  
  for (n in n_values) {
    
    cat("Running simulation for n =", n, "\n")
    
    results[[paste0("n_", n)]] <- simulate_means(
      n = n,
      reps = reps
    )
  }
  
  results
}
```

Here, \(n\) is the number of Standard Normal observations in one sample. The value `reps` is the number of repeated samples used to create the sampling distribution.

## Broad-Range Simulations

```{r}
set.seed(student_id)

broad_means <- run_simulations(
  n_values = broad_n_values,
  reps = reps
)
```

Each value of \(n\) produces 10,000 simulated sample means.

## Checking the Number of Simulations

```{r}
broad_simulation_check <- data.frame(
  sample_size_n = broad_n_values,
  number_of_sample_means = sapply(
    broad_means,
    length
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  broad_simulation_check,
  digits = 0,
  caption = "Broad-Range Simulation Counts"
)
```

Each sample size should have 10,000 simulated sample means.

## Saving the Broad-Range Sample Means

```{r}
convert_to_long_format <- function(
  means_list,
  n_values,
  range_label
) {
  
  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(seq_along(n_values), function(i) {
      
      data.frame(
        range = range_label,
        sample_size_n = n_values[i],
        repetition = seq_len(length(means_list[[i]])),
        sample_mean = means_list[[i]]
      )
    })
  )
}

broad_means_long <- convert_to_long_format(
  broad_means,
  broad_n_values,
  "broad"
)

write.csv(
  broad_means_long,
  "standard_normal_broad_sample_means.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

## Diagnostic Functions

```{r}
calculate_skewness <- function(x) {
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}

calculate_excess_kurtosis <- function(x) {
  mean((x - mean(x))^4) / sd(x)^4 - 3
}

calculate_outliers <- function(x) {
  
  q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25)
  q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75)
  iqr_value <- q3 - q1
  
  sum(
    x < q1 - 1.5 * iqr_value |
      x > q3 + 1.5 * iqr_value
  )
}

calculate_diagnostics <- function(
  means_list,
  n_values
) {
  
  simulated_means <- sapply(
    means_list,
    mean
  )
  
  simulated_se <- sapply(
    means_list,
    sd
  )
  
  theoretical_se <- population_sd / sqrt(n_values)
  
  tail_proportions <- sapply(
    seq_along(n_values),
    function(i) {
      
      mean(
        abs(
          means_list[[i]] - population_mean
        ) >
          3 * theoretical_se[i]
      )
    }
  )
  
  data.frame(
    sample_size_n = n_values,
    
    simulated_mean = simulated_means,
    
    theoretical_mean =
      rep(population_mean, length(n_values)),
    
    mean_error =
      simulated_means - population_mean,
    
    simulated_standard_error =
      simulated_se,
    
    theoretical_standard_error =
      theoretical_se,
    
    relative_standard_error_error =
      abs(
        simulated_se -
          theoretical_se
      ) / theoretical_se,
    
    skewness = sapply(
      means_list,
      calculate_skewness
    ),
    
    excess_kurtosis = sapply(
      means_list,
      calculate_excess_kurtosis
    ),
    
    outlier_count = sapply(
      means_list,
      calculate_outliers
    ),
    
    proportion_beyond_three_SE =
      tail_proportions
  )
}
```

## Broad-Range Diagnostics

```{r}
broad_diagnostics <- calculate_diagnostics(
  broad_means,
  broad_n_values
)

knitr::kable(
  broad_diagnostics,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Broad-Range Diagnostic Results"
)
```

The simulated mean should be close to 0, the simulated standard error should follow \(1/\sqrt{n}\), and skewness and excess kurtosis should be close to 0 for every \(n\).

## Broad-Range Histograms

```{r}
plot_n_values <- c(
  1, 10, 30, 100
)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (n in plot_n_values) {
  
  means <- broad_means[[paste0("n_", n)]]
  
  hist(
    means,
    breaks = 40,
    probability = TRUE,
    main = paste("Sampling Distribution, n =", n),
    xlab = "Sample mean",
    col = "lightblue",
    border = "white"
  )
  
  curve(
    dnorm(
      x,
      mean = population_mean,
      sd = population_sd / sqrt(n)
    ),
    add = TRUE,
    col = "red",
    lwd = 2
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

All of the histograms should be approximately bell-shaped because the original population is already normal. As \(n\) increases, the distributions should become narrower because the standard error decreases.

## Broad-Range Normal Q–Q Plots

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (n in plot_n_values) {
  
  means <- broad_means[[paste0("n_", n)]]
  
  qqnorm(
    means,
    main = paste("Normal Q–Q Plot, n =", n)
  )
  
  qqline(
    means,
    col = "red",
    lwd = 2
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The points should follow the red line closely for every value of \(n\), supporting the theoretical result that the sample mean is normal for every sample size.

## Broad-Range Standard-Error Comparison

```{r}
plot(
  broad_diagnostics$sample_size_n,
  broad_diagnostics$simulated_standard_error,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  log = "x",
  xlab = "Sample size n",
  ylab = "Standard deviation of sample means",
  main = "Simulated and Theoretical Standard Error"
)

lines(
  broad_diagnostics$sample_size_n,
  broad_diagnostics$theoretical_standard_error,
  type = "b",
  col = "red",
  pch = 17
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    "Simulated standard error",
    "Theoretical standard error"
  ),
  col = c("black", "red"),
  pch = c(19, 17),
  lty = 1
)
```

The simulated standard errors should follow the theoretical \(1/\sqrt{n}\) curve. Increasing \(n\) decreases the spread of the sample means but does not determine whether they are normal in this case.

## Choosing the Refinement Interval

The Standard Normal population is theoretically normal for every \(n\), so refinement is not necessary. This interval is included for visual confirmation.

```{r}
refinement_lower <- 1
refinement_upper <- 5

refined_n_values <- seq(
  refinement_lower,
  refinement_upper,
  by = 1
)

refined_n_values
```

## Fine-Grained Simulations

```{r}
set.seed(student_id)

refined_means <- run_simulations(
  refined_n_values,
  reps
)
```

## Fine-Grained Diagnostics

```{r}
refined_diagnostics <- calculate_diagnostics(
  refined_means,
  refined_n_values
)

knitr::kable(
  refined_diagnostics,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Fine-Grained Diagnostic Results"
)
```

## Comparing Refined Sample Sizes

```{r}
qq_correlations <- c()

for (i in 1:length(refined_n_values)) {
  
  n <- refined_n_values[i]
  
  means <- refined_means[[paste0("n_", n)]]
  
  probabilities <- (
    (1:length(means)) - 0.5
  ) / length(means)
  
  theoretical_quantiles <- qnorm(
    probabilities
  )
  
  qq_correlations[i] <- cor(
    sort(means),
    theoretical_quantiles
  )
}

refined_diagnostics$absolute_mean_error <-
  abs(refined_diagnostics$mean_error)

refined_diagnostics$absolute_standard_error_error <-
  abs(
    refined_diagnostics$simulated_standard_error -
      refined_diagnostics$theoretical_standard_error
  )

refined_diagnostics$qq_correlation <-
  qq_correlations
```

```{r}
refined_diagnostics$mean_error_rank <- rank(
  refined_diagnostics$absolute_mean_error,
  ties.method = "min"
)

refined_diagnostics$standard_error_rank <- rank(
  refined_diagnostics$absolute_standard_error_error,
  ties.method = "min"
)

refined_diagnostics$qq_rank <- rank(
  -refined_diagnostics$qq_correlation,
  ties.method = "min"
)

refined_diagnostics$total_score <-
  refined_diagnostics$mean_error_rank +
    refined_diagnostics$standard_error_rank +
    refined_diagnostics$qq_rank
```

```{r}
best_row <- which.min(
  refined_diagnostics$total_score
)

best_n <- refined_diagnostics$sample_size_n[best_row]

best_n
```

```{r}
comparison_table <- refined_diagnostics[
  order(refined_diagnostics$total_score),
]

knitr::kable(
  comparison_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Comparison of Refined Sample Sizes"
)
```

## Fine-Grained Histograms

The plots below show the lower refinement bound, the best-scoring value, and the upper refinement bound.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

refined_plot_values <- sort(

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
```

The histograms should all look approximately bell-shaped. The main change as \(n\) increases should be a decrease in spread, not a change from non-normal to normal.

## Selected Sample Size

The selected sample size is \(n=1\). Since the original population is already normal, the sample mean is normally distributed for every sample size. Increasing \(n\) reduces the standard error, but it is not needed to create normality.

## CLT Assumptions and Limitations

The observations are independent and identically distributed, and the Standard Normal population has a finite mean and finite variance. This is a favorable case because the original population is already normal. Therefore, this distribution does not show how the CLT handles a skewed or heavy-tailed population.

## Conclusion

The Standard Normal population is normal for every sample size \(n\), including \(n=1\). The simulations, histograms, Q–Q plots, and diagnostic values should all support this theoretical result. The main effect of increasing \(n\) is that the sampling distribution becomes narrower because its standard error decreases according to \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
